from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

    s=p.extract_text()

(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:3]))

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether optimization methods that improve generalization can simultaneously increase membership leakage.

The experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, several attack methods, and additional architectures. Five-run averages and standard deviations provide useful evidence that SAM can increase single-query attack accuracy.
Analyzing performance across test-example cohorts moves beyond aggregate accuracy and raises an interesting hypothesis about SAM’s benefits for atypical examples.

SharpReg is a simple optimization modification with substantial improvements against the evaluated attacks. On CIFAR-100, single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% to 59.64%, while test accuracy decreases from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central influence-entropy metric is not well defined as written. Influence scores can be negative, and Equation (3) divides by zero when all scores vanish. Appendix C.1 nevertheless assigns all-zero cases—2,153 of 10,000 test examples—to the highest-entropy bucket. Explicit preprocessing, a justified zero-influence convention, and sensitivity analyses are necessary to validate the proposed memorization spectrum.

The experiments do not establish that SAM’s gains arise from increased memorization. The influence scores were computed under SGD, and better performance on those cohorts could reflect improved representations or differences in difficulty and accuracy ceilings. Direct memorization measurements under SAM, targeted removal experiments, and measured sharpness would strengthen the proposed mechanism. The detailed cohort analysis is also confined to CIFAR-100.

The privacy conclusions require narrower scope and stronger evaluation. SAM decreases label-only attack accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 69.18% to 65.41%, with similar decreases across the other image architectures; its Purchase-100 single-query increase is only 0.29 percentage points, within the reported variability. These results support an attack-dependent pattern. Strong reference-model attacks such as LiRA, performance at low false-positive rates, and sensitivity to SAM’s perturbation radius are missing.

SharpReg’s proposed additional anti-overfitting mechanism is insufficiently justified. For xi < 1, Equation (5) is a positive rescaling of Equation (4), with lambda replaced by lambda/(1-xi). Although the appendix acknowledges a parameter reduction, the claimed distinct role of the added term as a proxy for early stopping needs comparisons controlling the effective sharpness coefficient, learning rate, and weight decay.

The attack tables contain a material inconsistency requiring reconciliation. Under balanced membership evaluation, the correctness attack defined in Equation (8) has accuracy approximately 50% + (training accuracy − test accuracy)/2. The CIFAR-100 SGD accuracies in Table 4 imply approximately 59.84%, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. Exact evaluation subset sizes and member/nonmember balancing are insufficiently specified to explain this discrepancy; variability across victim-training seeds is also unclear.

The claimed privacy–accuracy tradeoff is not convincingly competitive. In Table 4, SELENA exceeds the selected SharpReg configuration on CIFAR-100 in test accuracy (76.92% versus 76.14%) while achieving lower single-query and multi-query attack accuracies; it also dominates SharpReg on Texas-100. Comparisons against tuned early stopping and standard regularization at matched utility are needed, alongside compute measurements supporting the efficiency advantage.
